slides.title: Introduction
slides.description: The Red Flag Rule requires businesses and organizations to implement identity theft prevention program designed to detect the "Red Flags" of identity theft in their day-to-day operations, take steps to prevent the crime, and mitigate its damage. Red Flags are the potential patterns, practices, or specific activities indicating the possibility of identity theft.

slides.title: From a consumers perspective;...
slides.description:
• By 2022 there will have been more than 13.5 million victims of Identity theft in the U.S. alone.
  • The average time spent recovering from identity theft ranges from 330 hours to more than 600 hours.
  • The emotional impact of identity theft is similar to or likened to victim of a violent crime.
  • The cost to the economy is well in excess of $60 Billion dollars a year – everything that we buy costs more because of this issue.

slides.title: Why Red Flag legislation?
slides.description:
• The passage of the FACT Act was preceded by countless events highlighting ID Theft as a growing and pervasive problem.
  • Congressional hearings regarding reauthorization of Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) and its role in fighting ID theft took place.
  • The release of a report by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) that detailed the impact and scope of ID Theft as the fastest growing white collar crime in the U.S.
  • Articles in the newspapers and television programs relating to ID theft on nearly a daily basis brought the problem to the public's attention.

slides.title: FACT Act Red Flag Timeline
slides.description:
• The identity theft program includes: (1) establish and maintain guidelines regarding ID theft and Up-Date them regularly (2) Identify and detect Red Flags. (3) Responding appropriately to Red Flags that are detected. (4) Review with management annually regarding any such updates and changes to program.
  • The final rule was released by the combined regulatory agencies on October 31st, 2007.
  • The effective date was January 1st, 2008.

slides.title: Fact Act Requirements Section 315;
slides.description:
Requires consumer reporting agencies to notify parties requesting consumer reports of substantial address discrepancies … and to develop regulations providing guidance on “reasonable policies and procedures” for “financial institutions” i.e. automotive dealerships to follow upon receipt of a notice of address discrepancy including;

  • Formation of reasonable belief that the user knows identity of consumer; and
  • Reconciliation of the address with the consumer reporting agency that provided the notice if a continuing relationship is established.

slides.title: Develop and implement a written Identity Theft Prevention Program including reasonable policies and procedures to:
slides.description:
• Identify Red Flags
  • Detect Red Flags
  • Respond appropriately to Red Flags that are detected
  • Periodically update the Red Flag Program

slides.title: What is our role in all of this?
slides.description:
• We are required to do more than just get a copy of a driver's license.
  • We need to pay more attention to the Credit Bureau and look for notices and or any customer insertions.
  • Your main guide in detecting identity discrepancies is common sense.

slides.title: Some examples of red flags:
slides.description:
• Fraud or active duty alerts on a consumer report
  • Consumer report provides a notice of credit freeze
  • Address discrepancy contained in a consumer report or in the information provided
  • A consumer report indicates a pattern of activity that is inconsistent with the history and usual pattern of the applicant including a recent and significant increases in the volume of inquiries, a recent surge in established credit.
  • Relationships, material changes in the use of credit with respect to recently established credit relationships, and accounts that have been closed for cause or identified for abuse of account priviledges.
  • The address provided by the consumer is inconsistent with that provided by consumer reports.
  • If the social security number provided has been issued or is listed on the death master file.
  • Identifying information provided by the consumer is not consistent with personal identifying information provided, for example there is a lack of correlation between the social security number range and date of birth
  • The information provided is known, and associated with fraudulent activity.
  • the phone number on an application is the same as a number provided on a fraudulent application.
